trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, a $2 day-use ticket (in addition to the park entrance pass) is required to hike Old Rag from March through November, sold on Recreation.gov starting 30 days and again 5 days before each date — buy one before you go, and note the main parking lot has reduced capacity in 2026 due to an ongoing improvement project.
trails.didYouKnow: The famous rock scramble near the summit involves squeezing through narrow granite passages and is often considered the most strenuous popular day hike in the park.

trails.trailTip: The return climb is steeper than it looks on the way down — pace yourself and expect wet, slick rocks near the falls after rain.
trails.didYouKnow: At just 1.4 miles round trip, this is the shortest route in the park to a named waterfall, making it one of its most popular short hikes.

trails.trailTip: Hawksbill is the highest point in the park, so weather can shift fast — bring a layer even if it's warm at the trailhead.
trails.didYouKnow: At 4,051 feet, Hawksbill is Shenandoah's highest summit and is home to a small remnant population of high-elevation red spruce.

trails.trailTip: This full Whiteoak Canyon–Cedar Run circuit is rocky with several stream crossings and is rated very strenuous by NPS — budget most of a day, and expect wet feet.
trails.didYouKnow: The full loop passes seven named waterfalls in total — four on Whiteoak Run, three on Cedar Run — with the tallest dropping about 86 feet.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, some cliff faces near the summit close seasonally, typically May through July, to protect nesting peregrine falcons — stay on the marked trail and respect any posted closure.
trails.didYouKnow: At 4,010 feet, Stony Man is the park's second-highest peak, and its profile from below resembles a reclining face.

trails.trailTip: The rock scramble section requires hands-on climbing over exposed boulders — not recommended in wet or icy conditions.
trails.didYouKnow: Bearfence is one of the few spots in the park with a true 360-degree summit view without any tree cover.

trails.trailTip: The old mining ruins along the loop are fragile and partially collapsed — view them from the trail rather than climbing on the structures.
trails.didYouKnow: The loop passes remnants of the Old Rose River copper mine, which operated briefly in the early 1900s.

trails.trailTip: The Meadow Spring approach is steeper but shorter than the alternate route from Skyline Drive's Thornton Gap — pace the climb and enjoy the summit views over Panorama.
trails.didYouKnow: Mary's Rock overlooks Thornton Gap, one of only a few places where a highway (U.S. 211) cuts through the Blue Ridge inside the park.

trails.trailTip: The summit is a jumbled boulder field — wear sturdy shoes and watch your footing, especially with kids along.
trails.didYouKnow: The boulders atop Blackrock are actually ancient quartzite talus, remnants of the erosion-resistant rock that caps many Blue Ridge summits.

animals.whereToLook: Big Meadows and forested trail corridors throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, keep at least 150 feet (50 yards) from any bear, never approach for a photo, and store all food and scented items properly — bears here have one of the highest population densities in the East and some individuals near trails and campgrounds have become food-conditioned.
animals.didYouKnow: Shenandoah has one of the densest black bear populations in the eastern United States, despite the park's relatively small size.

animals.whereToLook: Big Meadows and open fields along Skyline Drive
animals.viewingTip: In late spring, watch for fawns bedded alone in tall grass — this is normal behavior, not abandonment, so admire from a distance and never touch or move one.
animals.didYouKnow: Big Meadows deer are famously unbothered by visitors, having grown accustomed to roadside traffic over decades.

animals.viewingTip: Slow down and watch from your car or the roadside — turkeys along Skyline Drive are used to traffic but can still startle if approached on foot.
animals.didYouKnow: Wild turkeys can run up to 25 mph and fly in short, powerful bursts despite their heavy build.

animals.whereToLook: Cliffs near Old Rag's summit and Stony Man Mountain
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, nesting cliffs near Old Rag and Stony Man close to visitor access seasonally, typically May through July — view falcons with binoculars from designated overlooks rather than the closed cliff faces.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrines were extirpated from Shenandoah by the mid-20th century due to DDT and were successfully reestablished through a hacking (release) program starting in the 1980s.

animals.whereToLook: Sunny rock outcrops on ridgelines like Old Rag and Bearfence
animals.viewingTip: If you see one basking, step back and give it a wide berth on the trail — it isn't aggressive if left alone, but never try to move or handle it.
animals.didYouKnow: Timber rattlesnakes are ambush predators that may stay coiled in the same basking spot for days at a time.

animals.whereToLook: Forested hollows away from main trail corridors
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are uncommon and brief — if you spot one, stay still and watch quietly with binoculars rather than following it into the brush.
animals.didYouKnow: Bobcats are largely solitary and territorial, marking their home range with scent rather than relying on sight of other bobcats.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky ledges and leaf litter near trail edges
animals.viewingTip: Copperheads blend in extremely well with leaf litter — watch your footing on rocky sections and give any snake you spot a wide berth rather than reaching near logs or rock crevices.
animals.didYouKnow: A copperhead's banded pattern is often compared to a stack of Hershey's Kisses, which helps it disappear against dappled forest floor light.

animals.viewingTip: If you hear a male's drumming display in spring, stay on the trail and enjoy the sound rather than searching the underbrush — grouse nest on the ground and a flushed hen may abandon eggs.
animals.didYouKnow: A ruffed grouse's drumming sound is made by rapidly beating its wings against the air, not by striking anything — it can be felt as a low thump from a distance.

animals.whereToLook: Meadow edges and forest clearings along Skyline Drive
animals.viewingTip: Watch from a distance with binoculars and never use calls or bait to draw one closer — coyotes that lose their wariness of people are more likely to end up in conflict.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes expanded into the Blue Ridge region over the last century and now fill part of the ecological role once played by wolves in the eastern U.S.
